body:
Hey there, thanks for writing this up. Consensus around this solution is blocked on WHATWG policy of multiple implementers planning to implement it. Right now only Chrome has a dialog implementation, and we do not support the change, so we'd need to see intent to ship for the dialog feature itself, plus this change, by two other implementers before we could consider the change to the spec.

In other words, it's best if the spec reflect the reality of the single implementation that does exist, instead of reflecting zero implementations as it would do after landing this PR.
That was discussed in detail in the previous threads.

I forgot to mention, there's a separate question as to whether we should remove dialog from the spec entirely. For a while it looked like Gecko was going to land an implementation, but that didn't happen and now it's back to being Chrome-only, which is not great (and leads to dynamics such as this one, where we're debating having the spec match 0 vs. 1 browsers).
I support @stevefaulkner 's position. There appears to be a strong consensus building among people knowledgeable about accessibility that focus should be placed on it. I add my voice.
So now Firefox has the dialog element in Nightly and pursuing to keep moving it forward, Can we merge the changes here?
No, this change does not have multi-implementer interest. See https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/4184#issuecomment-440326010

@domenic I'm not sure I understand, there is multi-implementer interest as per #4937 (all engines want to support dialog). And as per OP both Apple and Mozilla want this change. What's lacking multi-implementer interest is Chrome's position, as far as I can tell.

> And as per OP both Apple and Mozilla want this change.

I don't think we can count Apple in this calculation, as they don't support dialog at all.
But they have expressed implementer interest, which is what matters per the Working Mode, no?

I think it's more subtle than that. Expressing interest in a normative change of a feature you don't implement is not sufficient to count as implementer interest, in my opinion. Especially given our fraught history with dialog having "interest" but no implementation for many years, I believe we really need to err on the side of actual implementation interest, i.e. the working mode's

> The support from implementers should be of the form “we would like to implement this soon” and not just “this seems like a reasonable idea”.

As I've mentioned before, for this reason I'm also open to removing dialog entirely until we can get a serious interoperable-across-multiple-implementers implementation. I think that would be better than Firefox implementing one thing for this focus issue, and Chrome implementing another, and the spec picking one or the other of them based on what someone chimes in from the sidelines to say they prefer.
So for Firefox this is pretty important, so I'd love it if maybe @mfreed7 @josepharhar could give some more detail as to why this cannot be changed, but Chrome appears pretty flexible on #5678.

I'm not aware of any reason why this can't be changed, but I'm also not an expert on the dialog element in the first place.
As I said in [this comment](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/5678#issuecomment-739965398), I'd basically have to try  implementing it and hope I don't break any websites.

The reason we have been historically opposed to this in Chrome is that it is contrary to how native dialogs behave. (That is, the current specification matches native dialogs, and the proposed change fails to do so.) There is a long history here, starting in https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=23366 and continuing in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1929, which is worth reading if the DOM team would like to change Chrome's historical policy stance on this.
Good to hear that this can be possibly changed, FWIW, I'll help out with tests.

> The reason we have been historically opposed to this in Chrome is that it is contrary to how native dialogs behave. (That is, the current specification matches native dialogs, and the proposed change fails to do so.) There is a long history here, starting in https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=23366 and continuing in #1929, which is worth reading if the DOM team would like to change Chrome's historical policy stance on this.

Thanks, I hadn't read #1929 at all. After doing some light skimming, it sounds like [the reporter decided that this shouldn't be done anymore](https://codereview.chromium.org/2532983004/#msg14) and that https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2197 could be an alternative way to fix this?

>The reason we have been historically opposed to this in Chrome is that it is contrary to how native dialogs behave.

While I can respect the desire to keep with native behavior, web developers cram so much more / different types of content into web dialogs that matching native behavior isn't always ideal. For instance [this monster `<dialog>`](https://scottaohara.github.io/testing/html-dialog/tos-dialog.html) based on real content found in the wild.

The variability of where focus can start in web dialogs creates unpredictability in how they can be interacted with, and how much content will be announced, or potentially *not* announced to screen reader users / where focus will land and how much content can potentially scroll out of view for sighted users. Allowing focus to always start at the top of a dialog (similar to a standard web page), rather than being forced to the first focusable element, would allow all users to interact with the dialog in a consistently meaningful way.

This is a constant issue in the accessibility and usability of custom dialogs, and one that will continue to require additional effort from developers if the native dialog can't be adjusted, because of historical reasons.

If the default behavior will not be changed, then I would request that a feature (attribute?) be added to allow the dialog to receive initial focus, as there is a clear and consistently expressed desire for this behavior here and in previous threads.

> If the default behavior will not be changed, then I would request that a feature (attribute?) be added to allow the dialog to receive initial focus, as there is a clear and consistently expressed desire for this behavior here and in previous threads.

Is this what https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/2197 is proposing?

If so, then my apologies for my slip in connecting the dots there.

(re)reading this again, if it's saying that if `skipInitialFocus:true` will achieve the desired behavior... focus will move to the dialog itself, unless it contained an element with the `autofocus` attribute, where focus would be expected to move to that element... then yes, this does seem like it would meet the 2nd-choice request to have an official way to opt-out of the native focus behavior.  

Still would prefer that just be the default behavior, and use `autofocus` for situations where developers specifically want a particular element to be focused by default. But would appreciate that something be in place so as to point developers to what they may well need to do instead.

We are trying to make this happen :) 

- [x] At least two implementers are interested (and none opposed):
   * Firefox is interested
   * Chrome sounds also flexible for this change 
- [x] [Tests](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt) are written and can be reviewed and commented upon at:
   * Tests are included in this Firefox patch: https://phabricator.services.mozilla.com/D109950, will be merged automatically to WPT once it's landed. 
- [x] [Implementation bugs](https://github.com/whatwg/meta/blob/main/MAINTAINERS.md#handling-pull-requests) are filed:
   * Chrome: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1193482
   * Firefox: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1701230

ping @domenic @josepharhar

Although @josepharhar's team is the one making the final call here for Chromium, and not me, I continue to believe this is the wrong path as I stated a few months ago in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/4184#issuecomment-740047054, as it diverges `<dialog>` from native dialogs. Something like #2197 seems more acceptable instead of breaking the default behavior.

Also, recall that dialogs are not focusable areas today, so the change here would be pretty large with more serious compat implications. #1929 digs into that more, and also discusses how `<dialog>` is poorly suited for cases like menus (where not focusing the first-focusable child makes sense; instead the menu element should be focusable).

I didn't go through the [webkit's discussion](https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=23366) because it was a long thread.....However, it looks like the recent agreement on that is this [comment](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1929#issuecomment-272527090) made @cookiecrook, so I don't think we still have any concerns left with native dialogs. 

Also, note that in the past, we had reached a general consensus about this change in #1929, although dbeam had moved on from working on Chrome.

In general we shouldn't rely on year-old affirmations from people who may or may not still be working on the relevant area of code; if you're trying to land a change now, it's good idea to get interest now.

@josepharhar could you please provide an update for Chrome? @cookiecrook has your thinking on this perhaps changed since https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/4184#issue-232225311 or do you still agree with that? As I understand it Firefox's accessibility team still thinks this is the way to go.

At the last triage meeting we discussed this issue and the conclusion was that we needed a clearer statement of use cases and user journeys, instead of focusing on this specific solution. In particular we want to compare those user journeys to native dialogs (of the type Firefox already implements in its native UI) so we could compare how Firefox and others solve such journeys for native dialogs with any proposed solution for the HTML element. So the ball is currently in @sefeng211's court to collate those for the group.
I'll defer to domenic on this one. I don't have much context/insight on this, and the only reason I will say no is if the change breaks existing tests/websites.

At the last HTML triage meeting, folks requested input on this issue from accessibility folks at Microsoft. After some discussion, our group's conclusion was that:

* With any choice, there are tradeoffs and differing user preferences. We're aiming for the most reasonable baseline/default.
* If `dialog` was used strictly in the sense of OS platform dialogs (e.g. some string and OK/cancel buttons), it would be preferable and expected to place focus on one of those commands.
* But because the HTML `dialog` element can have varying different content models in active use, and because of potential accessibility issues, it would be best to set focus on the dialog itself by default. An exemplary accessibility issue would be a scenario where a screen magnifier user is sent to some random link in a long and complex dialog, and loses context or even awareness of contents that come before that first focusable element.
* Web developers can and should think critically about (and test!) whether setting focus to the `dialog` is the best experience for their given use case, and can use available primitives to send focus elsewhere as appropriate. But for the swath of web developers who haven't put in this level of consideration, sending focus to the `dialog` itself is a preferable baseline/default. _(Aside: perhaps a new [`delegatesfocus`](https://open-ui.org/components/popup.research.explainer) attribute would be helpful here for developers who know the first focusable element should be appropriate for their suite of dialogs.)_

For transparency, this discussion was not based on independent user research tailored to this question, but on prior art/knowledge in the space. People with disabilities (and users of assistive technologies) were participants in the discussion, and their opinions are their own vs necessarily representative of all people with their disability. :)

Hi @melanierichards, it's helpful that you got an opinion on the desired end state out of your internal stakeholders, but the next steps we needed were a better sense of the use cases and user journeys.

You hinted at such use cases with "But because the HTML dialog element can have varying different content models in active use", contrasting them with (what the dialog element is currently designed for) "If dialog was used strictly in the sense of OS platform dialogs (e.g. some string and OK/cancel buttons)".

Could you or the stakeholders you consulted expand upon such "dialogs" that don't match the OS platform/HTML spec usage of the term, what the desired user experience is in such situations, and how native apps (on mobile or desktop) behave in those situations? A concrete example would be ideal, e.g. some non-dialog "dialog" that appears in Microsoft Office perhaps, and what the focus behavior is for it. Then, once we have such a concrete use case, we could continue from the place where we left off, and discuss whether `<dialog>` with non-OS-dialog focus behavior is the best way to bring that pattern to the web, or whether there are other solutions for the use case.

> A concrete example would be ideal, e.g. some non-dialog "dialog" that appears in Microsoft Office perhaps, and what the focus behavior is for it.

As an example, this relatively complex dialog (maybe it meets the definition of "long and complex" from your message?) focuses the first control for me in Microsoft Outlook (the dropdown), instead of focusing the dialog itself:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/617481/117057849-ee493800-aceb-11eb-8b1f-da71b06c5913.png)

Given your statement

> An exemplary accessibility issue would be a scenario where a screen magnifier user is sent to some random link in a long and complex dialog, and loses context or even awareness of contents that come before that first focusable element.

I'd be curious to find how screen magnifier users find the experience of using that dialog in Microsoft Outlook.

Apologies for the misunderstanding @domenic, thought that was a general call to us for input w/r/t accessibility considerations and the question about OS paradigms was a parallel track of investigation.

Are you _only_ concerned with use cases in OS platform / native app environments? If we're pulling examples we should probably consider how the `dialog` element is used in practice on the web as well. We examined this through the lens of "if you can't control how web devs will (mis)use this element, what is the most reasonable starting point that more thoughtful authors can build on top of?" IIRC someone mentioned `dialog` being used for a TOS agreement flow. That would be a good example of inappropriately pushing initial focus down to a link somewhere in the contents of that TOS.

FWIW, I actually don't think the current definition of `dialog` precludes long and complex contents:

> The dialog element represents a part of an application that a user interacts with to perform a task, for example a dialog box, inspector, or window.

Somewhat orthogonal but perhaps this text could/should be more prescriptive to help authors understand what is appropriate.

> Are you only concerned with use cases in OS platform / native app environments? [...] We examined this through the lens of "if you can't control how web devs will (mis)use this element, what is the most reasonable starting point that more thoughtful authors can build on top of?"

Yes, generally. We don't write the spec to handle misuse cases; we instead design it for when it's used in a valid way. After all, people can use `<h1>` to represent big bold text, but that has bad impacts (for accessibility, among other things) and so we disallow it as part of the conformance requirements for writing valid HTML, and we don't change the behavior or accessibility mappings of `<h1>` to cater to such misuses.

> IIRC someone mentioned dialog being used for a TOS agreement flow. That would be a good example of inappropriately pushing initial focus down to a link somewhere in the contents of that TOS.

This is a perfect example of a use case we can examine in more detail. Here is an example of a TOS agreement flow dialog in Windows (grabbed off Google images):
 ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/617481/117062778-dd032a00-acf1-11eb-9a0b-18c30524def1.png)

Here the focused control is the first focusable control in the dialog, i.e. the scrollable TOS itself, not the dialog. That again seems like the correct behavior, and one we'd want to preserve on the web.

> FWIW, I actually don't think the current definition of dialog precludes long and complex contents:

I totally agree. I've given a couple examples so far of long, complex dialogs that meet the spec's definition where the expected behavior is to focus the first focusable control. I'd love to see some cases that meet the spec's definition (e.g. a dialog box, inspector, or window) where macOS, Windows, Android, or iOS focus the dialog itself, instead of focusing the first focusable control.

> As an example, this relatively complex dialog (maybe it meets the definition of "long and complex" from your message?) focuses the first control for me in Microsoft Outlook (the dropdown), instead of focusing the dialog itself:

In HTML, wouldn't the first focusable element be the tabs rather than the dropdown?

> Here the focused control is the first focusable control in the dialog, i.e. the scrollable TOS itself, not the dialog.

If the text were not in a scrollable region and were textual content of the dialog itself, the first focusable item could be a link in the middle of the text or an accept button at the bottom which would cause the text itself to be skipped.

---

It is easy for people to opt in to focusing something by default with `autofocus`, but there's currently no way to opt-out of autofocusing the wrong thing and force focus to go to the dialog.

> In HTML, wouldn't the first focusable element be the tabs rather than the dropdown?

It depends! In Windows, or at least in the control set Outlook and other Win32 apps use, tabs are not focusable in the normal way, and require a different set of keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+Tab and friends) to navigate.

> If the text were not in a scrollable region and were textual content of the dialog itself, the first focusable item could be a link in the middle of the text or an accept button at the bottom which would cause the text itself to be skipped.

Yeah, that'd be a pretty bad design for a dialog, I agree!

> It is easy for people to opt in to focusing something by default with autofocus, but there's currently no way to opt-out of autofocusing the wrong thing and force focus to go to the dialog.

Recall the purpose of the last few threads is to find a case where the correct thing to do is to focus the dialog. So far nobody has been able to exhibit any operating system dialog where that's the case; the gestures in that direction (namely, "long and complex dialogs" and "TOS dialogs") have been shown to instead, when we find real examples, work by focusing the first focusable control.

If we can find an example of an OS dialog (or other control meeting the spec's description, e.g. inspector or window) where that's a good behavior, then we can start digging into how to bring such a pattern to the web. But we still haven't gotten to that step!
Are you asserting that if nobody can find a native OS dialog that receives focus, that this issue should be closed?

> In Windows, or at least in the control set Outlook and other Win32 apps use, tabs are not focusable in the normal way, and require a different set of keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+Tab and friends) to navigate.

In Win32, tab controls are definitely focusable (similar to list boxes; the control gets focus and the items are navigable with arrow keys).

> > If the text were not in a scrollable region and were textual content of the dialog itself, the first focusable item could be a link in the middle of the text or an accept button at the bottom which would cause the text itself to be skipped.
> 
> Yeah, that'd be a pretty bad design for a dialog, I agree!

From what I've seen on the web, it's very rare to have separate text boxes for long form, non-editable content. A TOS agreement is normally just "content in the document", with no explicitly separate focusable region. In contrast, in native apps, that would normally be in a text box. While I normally agree we should try to mirror native behavour as much as possible, this is one case where I'm not sure we can use native use cases to make a good decision about web behaviour because the common design patterns for things like long form text differ.

> the gestures in that direction (namely, "long and complex dialogs" and "TOS dialogs") have been shown to instead, when we find real examples, work by focusing the first focusable control.

If the prevailing pattern on the web was to put long form text in focusable controls like it is in native apps, that might suggest we should do the same on the web. But at least as far as I've seen, that's not the prevailing pattern: web and native are just different in this respect.

Another thing to consider is that native apps usually focus some control in *any* window they open, whether that be the main window, a dialog or some other kind of window. In contrast, web documents, whether that be normal loading, opening a new window or opening a new tab, just focus the document unless autofocus is set. Right or wrong, that has resulted in specific patterns, expectations and behaviour by authors, assistive technology, etc. The main counter-argument to this proposed change is that we should be consistent with native dialogs, but the web is already inconsistent with native windows (in addition to the inconsistencies outlined in my previous comment).

> Are you asserting that if nobody can find a native OS dialog that receives focus, that this issue should be closed?

I think that's probably a reasonable direction. If we have no examples of native dialogs where focus should go to the dialog, then there's no motivation for bringing such funcitonality to the web's `<dialog>` element, as doing so would create an experience that's at odds with the purpose of `<dialog>` (to represent a dialog/window/inspector).

> From what I've seen on the web, it's very rare to have separate text boxes for long form, non-editable content. A TOS agreement is normally just "content in the document", with no explicitly separate focusable region.

This is why it's so important to focus on use cases. If the use case is "TOS dialogs" (or generally "dialogs with lots of text, some of which might be focusable") then there are two ways we could solve this:

1. Web developers follow the same pattern as native dialogs, e.g. by creating a scrollable/focusable text area for the TOS.

2. Web developers write dialogs that mismatch native dialogs, and don't have a separate TOS focusable area for that text. Then, we'd have to change the spec and browsers to focus the dialog itself to compensate for this.

We see here we have two ways of accomplishing a good experience and user journey. However, the first one is better according to the priority of constituencies: it gives users a symmetric experience across all dialogs they encounter, native and web. The second approach might be easier for authors, since it involves less elements, but authors are lower on the priority of constituencies hierarchy than users are.

This ties in to the general principle that we design HTML elements and their interaction semantics for when they are used correctly, not when they are used incorrectly. As I said above,

> After all, people can use `<h1>` to represent big bold text, but that has bad impacts (for accessibility, among other things) and so we disallow it as part of the conformance requirements for writing valid HTML, and we don't change the behavior or accessibility mappings of `<h1>` to cater to such misuses.

Similarly, people can create a web dialog where the first focusable element is way down in the dialog. But this has bad impacts (for accessibility, among other things), and so we should disallow it as part of the conformance requirements for writing valid HTML, instead of changing the behavior of `<dialog>` to give a worse user experience by default.

I'm coming at this issue as a screen reader user, accessibility tester and ex developer.
I don't feel it's always appropriate for HTML to mirror native OS behaviour, since users, and particularly screen reader users, interact with these two paradigms in very different ways. For one thing, the structure of native dialogs can be tightly controlled, which means that the dialog content can be fed to screen readers without the user having to do anything; whereas users are generally expected to interact more with HTML documents by using a virtual/review cursor to examine the content.
When a new HTML document is loaded, the focus is placed on the body, which positions the virtual cursor at the top of the document so that the user can begin reading from there.
But when a dialog is displayed, the placement of the virtual cursor is a hit and miss affair: if the dialog receives focus, then the user can begin reading from the top of the dialog, which is consistent with the user experience when a new document loads. But if the focus is moved to a control within the dialog, the user must then move the virtual cursor backwards to find and read from the beginning of the dialog. This may cause particular problems for deafblind users who rely on Braille displays: even if the dialog is constructed in a way that causes the screen reader to vocalise its complete content, this may well not be the most effective way for deafblind users to engage with the dialog.

I don't think I have anything new to add here, but I'd like to echo some of the thoughts of other commenters.

In my experience the dialog should receive focus unless explicitly chosen by the developer to do otherwise. Which element should receive focus is very context and task dependent, therefore making a best guess effort what to focus may often have a less than great outcome. 

As has been said further up the thread, the norms on the web around how dialogs are used, and for what type of content, are different to native. The worst case of a link in the middle of a large scrollable region automatically receiving focus, is a bad experience for all users. Context gets lost for users of assistive tech, and there is unnecessary and/or surprising scrolling for everyone else.

Some way to opt out of the first focusable element behaviour may work, but that makes for an awkward and easily forgotten API. For these reasons, I think focusing the dialog is the desirable default.

I (working on @Webkit’s `<dialog>` implementation) support this proposal for these reasons:
1. This matches the precedent of focusing the first autofocusable element, or document.body when not present
2. This still leaves the possibility of opting in focusing the first focusable element via the `autofocus` attribute if needed, while not forcing this behavior
3. the behavior of focusing the first focusable element can be bogus in cases where that element is scrolled out of view (e.g. a ToS dialog), see example in: https://www.scottohara.me/blog/2019/03/05/open-dialog.html#ux-and-accessibility-of-modal-dialogs
4. There is wide consensus for this change among accessibility-focused professionals (including screen reader developers and browser implementors) that this change will result in an improved experience for assistive technology users.

Chrome’s original argument against this proposal was that is does match native dialogs (alert/confirm/prompt) or OS-wide dialogs. I believe `<dialog>` use cases much more diverse than that, and focusing the first possible element may not be appropriate as shown in 3. Opt-in may still be possible via the `autofocus` attribute.
This has agreement between Gecko and WebKit, raising it for the triage meeting to let others know.

I just wanted to post something here so folks didn't think the Chromium team is ignoring this issue. We've been having some internal discussions to come to an agreement on a position. Our goal is to do the right thing for accessibility users, but we're not quite convinced exactly which option is best at this point. Our plan is to do a bit of research to see what actually happens in the wild today, and which option would be best for both AT and non-AT users. I promise to post back here in ~3 weeks with an update, and I apologize for the delay. If anyone already has some data (not anecdata, please) to inform this discussion, that would be super-helpful.

Curious what kind of data you are looking for? It is fundamentally a UX question, so there will be an element of subjectivity. How does the advice of experts and users in this thread not constitute data? 

We can surely prove by contradiction that focusing the dialog by default is the correct choice, since focusing the first interactive element has glaring issues in the "ToS dialog" scenario. 

If we hypothetically fast forward 3 weeks, and there is an absence of data, what is your proposed path forward?

@jcsteh @nt1m and I had some discussion about this elsewhere and there were some things that warrant further consideration I think:

* Should `show()` and `showModal()` have different behaviors? Currently they both focus, but perhaps the former should be more of an ARIA alert rather than alertdialog (i.e., not focus at all).
* If we continue to give `shodwModal()` focus behavior because this matches native dialogs, perhaps we should constrain it to the first form control to avoid focusing hyperlinks in a TOS and such. After all, native dialogs have buttons there.* And we probably need to fallback to focusing the dialog itself for the purposes of AT. (The reason we're considering this is because we use `<dialog>` for dialogs in Firefox and we'd probably add `autofocus` to the first form control if it wasn't focused by default. If we also clarify the specification to make it clear that this is what `<dialog>` is for (it currently suggests it could be for an entire application window...) that could work for us.)

(*It seems we also have a "button" type in the specification of sorts, but form-associated custom elements don't partake in it. This seems to be mainly used so they get to avoid supplying values during form submission and get to be valid as descendants of `canvas` elements.)

@annevk 
>Should `show()` and `showModal()` have different behaviors? Currently they both focus, but perhaps the former should be more of an ARIA alert rather than alertdialog (i.e., not focus at all).

This would be a pretty significant change since an `alert` is not a type of dialog, wouldn't it?   

HTML really only has two of the three types of dialogs (per ARIA roles/modality) spec'd at this point.  

1. non-modal dialogs are covered by `show()`, `role=dialog aria-modal=false`

2. `showModal()` is presently what many developers want for the variety of custom dialogs they need to create now with `role=dialog aria-modal=true`. 

3. alert dialog, which authors would still need to be modal, so would have to add `role=alertdialog` to their `<dialog>` invoked by `showModal()`.  An `alertdialog` being more in line with what it sounds like you / Firefox might be looking for, per the rest of your comment.

Is HTML open to creating a `showAlertDialog()` (or whatever it needs to be called) to allow for the three different scenarios that devs may need?  Or would it just be expected developers add `role=alertdialog` to the native `<dialog>` that needs to behave as a `role=alertdialog` (which seems quite reasonable as well).

Using the `autofocus` attribute gives developers control over a specific interactive element to receive focus by default, allowing for a consistent default of the dialog, otherwise (itself).  I don't see why there would need to be a change to the description of what the `<dialog>` element can be used for, especially in a way that would limit it from being used in how many developers need it. That doesn't seem like it would be a helpful change for web developers?

As a screen reader user, I really appreciate the points @domenic has raised and am quite confused by many points made by other accessibility devs.

I have some questions that might clear up some of my confusion, and I hope, help move the conversation forward with more common understanding.

#### Question 1 about nature of dialog focusability

What is the nature of the proposed focusability for dialogs? Does this proposal make dialog elements focusable elements in the same way that inputs are focusable? Or, would they be only programmatically focusable? Under what conditions could a dialog receive focus?

#### Question 2 about screen reader behavior assumptions

Given the lack of native precedent, what assumptions are being made about how screen readers would behave if a dialog were to receive focus?

Several comments suggest screen reader behavior when a dialog receives focus would be similar to screen reader behavior when the body element receives focus. I am not aware of an informal set of conventions for behavior in this circumstance, let alone a formal definition, and currently, there are significant variations across screen readers as well as inconsistencies within specific screen readers. So, for me, this comparison yields more questions and concerns than clarity. Without more clarity about this, how do we know that focusing the dialog will not lead to problematic screen reader behaviors or variations across screen readers that would create a fresh set of interop problems for web developers?

#### Question 3 about options considered

Since as @domenic points out, focusing a window container would be a new paradigm unique to web, have we considered any other potential new paradigms that might serve the accessibility use cases with possibly less complexity for assistive technology developers and users? Perhaps instead of hoisting more change on users, including assistive technology developers, we should consider putting more of the burden on implementers?

Accessibility use cases for when the dialog opens and author has not specified a starting point:
* screen mag users want to see the top left (in LTR)
* Screen reader users want to read from top
* others?

I can imagine a lot of ways that browsers could make the above happen without creating a new web-specific paradigm of focusing on a window container.

@mcking65 (et al who interested)

**Re: question 1**
The intent/hope/desire is to make them programmatically focusable by default, but to not have them take part in the focus order of the web page.  A dialog could receive initial focus when invoked, and this seems a reasonable default so long as a developer hadn't specified another element to instead send focus to.  Regardless of one's feelings on this, a fallback for this behavior *will be necessary* to mitigate against authors not including any focusable elements within a dialog, as there is presently no requirement that authors must do so. There are even real world situations where a modal dialog may be necessary, but should not provide a mechanism for users to dismiss (e.g., a dialog that indicates a loading message, where the content 'beneath' the dialog is updating and all users are prevented from accessing until the loading is complete - in which case the dialog could then auto-dismiss and allow everyone on their merry way).

**Re: question 2**
I can understand why you would assume that some people here may be making assumptions on how screen readers might behave.  Making custom dialogs focusable and having consistent experiences can be quite difficult (though also not impossible). However, it's really easy to test the dialog element, especially with Safari's Tech Preview shipping it, it being in Chrome (PC, Android, macOS), and in Firefox by turning on the dialog element's flag.  For instance, here are test cases for how screen readers presently behave when focusing a link or a text input in a dialog, and comparing those initial reading announcements with if the dialog element itself receives initial focus.

focusing a link first:
https://scottaohara.github.io/testing/html-dialog/just-dialog.html

focusing a text input first:
https://scottaohara.github.io/testing/html-dialog/first-input.html

In regards to problematic screen reader behaviors or variations, well, see the results I posted in the linked demos. Nothing is perfect right now, even if sending focus to a focusable element by default.  Regardless of where this conversation finally ends up, behaviors need to be spruced up in either case. They each have their problems and benefits. 


**Re: question 3**
Agreed, the concept of focusing a _window_ is different... but focusing a containing element within a web page is not new on the web, at all.  People do it all the time with skip links - focusing on the main element or sending focus to a menu container or a tabpanel. It happens frequently.  A web dialog exists in the web page itself, it's not a new window / browser window, and even though the spec presently says it cannot have a tabindex=-1 specified on it... well... it works as I demonstrated in my test case. Focus can be set to the dialog and content will be read aloud as with other focusable containers.  Again, we will _need_ this sort of behavior anyway since if a dialog can be used without containing a focusable element then presently some screen readers, like JAWS, will not auto-enter the dialog. The virtual cursor will remain on the control that invokes the dialog, and JAWS can continue to just read the contents of the page that has now been obscured by the dialog.  See https://scottaohara.github.io/testing/html-dialog/no-focusable-element.html


**Re: additional concerns**
We have all talked a lot about how screen readers will announce and behave with initial focus placement.  But we need to also keep in mind that there are benefits for sighted keyboard, low vision, and people with motor disabilities in making sure a dialog consistently allows people to start reading and navigate it from the top.  E.g., per the TOS example, where the first focusable element is nowhere near the top of a dialog's content, the dialog will have scrolled all previous content out of view to ensure that the focused element will be visible.  Even in smaller dialogs, where there might be a heading and a paragraph or two of content explaining the dialog at the start – keeping in mind users who zoom (whether that be to 200% or 400% per WCAG related success criteria), much of the instructional content can end up scrolled out of view as the browser ensures that the focused element will be visible.  Essentially, creating situations where if the first focusable element is not the dialog, or at the top of the dialog, then the dialog content will have to scroll.  While this is not necessarily a blocking issue, it puts additional effort on these users to navigate back to the top of the dialog to then be able to parse it from the start.  



Anyway, I hope that helps with some of your questions, Matt.  I hope my explanations and testing and results help put some context to things that people have been talking about, and will be useful to others here who might not have been able to test these things for themselves.

Status update:

A few of us (including myself, @scottaohara from Microsoft. @jcsteh from Mozilla, and others) got together to work out the issues with initial dialog focus. There were reasonable concerns. We gathered everything together and ended up with this proposal: https://github.com/whatwg/html/wiki/dialog--initial-focus,-a-proposal

The discussion has been very valuable. Our end goal is to pull improvements from this discussion into the specification and implementations. Doing so should effectively result in this PR being closed, and would finish out the original issues it was trying to resolve (#1929 and #2197).

Note that all browsers are currently shipping some form of initial focus in dialog. Firefox was satisfied with the direction of the discussion, and as a result, they started shipping `<dialog>` in Firefox 98. Safari 15.4 and Chrome/Edge already ship as well. 

The discussion needs to continue on these issues we uncovered: #2171, #5667, #7707, #7708, #7709 and #7710. We hope that resolving these issues and others will lead to improvements in the spec and implementations. Please feel free to comment on these issues or open new ones.
